parsed_answer.content:
In system design and high-performance data processing, the inverted index serves as the foundational data structure behind enterprise full-text search engines like Apache Lucene, Elasticsearch, and custom in-memory text retrieval systems in Java. Traditional relational databases excel at structured queries (e.g., exact matches, range queries on B-Trees), but scanning raw text columns for specific words requires $O(N)$ full table scans, which is disastrously slow for large corpora. An inverted index flips this relationship: instead of mapping documents to lists of words (a forward index), it maps every unique token (word) to a specialized posting list containing the document IDs and exact positions where that token appears.

Building a high-throughput inverted index requires a deep understanding of text analysis pipelines, tokenization, normalization, and memory management. When raw text streams into a Java application, it passes through a series of filters. Tokenizers split character streams by whitespace or punctuation; normalizers lowercase characters, strip accents, and apply stemming algorithms (like the Porter Stemmer) to reduce words to their root forms (e.g., running, runs, ran -> run). Once tokens are extracted, they are registered in a term dictionary, typically backed by a trie, prefix tree, or sorted array, which points to posting lists optimized for compression algorithms like Elias-Fano or Variable Byte Encoding.

O(Term Frequency) direct lookup via dictionary

items: Term Dictionary & Lexicon: The dictionary maps unique terms to metadata, including document frequency (DF) and pointers to the posting list on disk or in off-heap memory. In high-performance search engines, this dictionary is kept in RAM using FSTs (Finite State Transducers) for extreme space efficiency.

Posting Lists: A posting list stores the sorted array of document IDs (DocIDs) matching a term, often accompanied by term frequencies (TF) and positional data for phrase queries. Delta encoding (storing differences between consecutive DocIDs rather than absolute IDs) is heavily used to minimize memory footprints.

Scoring Algorithms (BM25/TF-IDF): When multiple search terms are provided, the inverted index intersects or unions posting lists. Scoring formulas like Okapi BM25 evaluate term frequency, inverse document frequency, and field-length normalization to rank results by relevance.

parsed_answer.content: When implementing custom inverted indices in high-concurrency Java applications, avoid storing millions of posting lists inside standard heap-allocated `ArrayList<Integer>` structures. Unboxed object overhead and garbage collection pause times (Stop-The-World) will degrade throughput. Instead, use primitive arrays, off-heap byte buffers (Direct ByteBuffers), or established engines like Apache Lucene, which handles memory-mapped files and delta-compressed posting lists natively.
